subject: Critical Thinking
title: The Law of Large Numbers: Why Casinos Always Win
description: A quick win: understand The Law of Large Numbers: Why Casinos Always Win.

hook.text: A gambler can win big on one night. The casino wins big every night. The difference: the casino plays enough hands.

buildup.text: The law of large numbers: as you repeat a random event, the average outcome converges to the expected value.

discovery.text: Flip a coin 10 times: you might get 7 heads. Flip it 10,000 times: you'll get very close to 50% heads.

twist.text: This doesn't mean outcomes 'balance out.' Each flip is independent. The past doesn't affect the future.

climax.text: Insurance, investing, and A/B testing all exploit this law. With enough repetitions, randomness becomes predictable.

punchline.text: One bet is a gamble. A thousand bets is a business model.

quiz.question: What does the law of large numbers guarantee?
options: Average outcomes converge to expected value with many repetitions

details.summary: The law of large numbers states that as sample size increases, the average outcome converges on the expected value. This is why casinos always profit in the long run despite individual winners.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding this law explains why short-term randomness misleads and why large sample sizes are essential for reliable conclusions.
takeaways: Large samples converge on expected averages
Small samples are unreliable and produce extreme results
Casinos profit from volume, not from winning every hand

faq.question: How does the law of large numbers explain casino profitability?
faq.answer: Each game has a small house edge. In the short run, any player might win. But across millions of bets, the average outcome converges on the house edge with mathematical certainty. Volume eliminates the casino's risk.

faq.question: Why do people draw strong conclusions from small samples?
faq.answer: We intuitively expect small samples to be representative of the population, but they are not. A restaurant with three five-star reviews could easily be mediocre. The law of large numbers only applies to large, representative samples.
